indexableObject.name: The Religious Societies Act, 1880

dc.description.abstract.value:
Summary of the Religious Societies Act, 1880


Key Provisions
1.	Jurisdiction and Exemptions:- Applies to the whole of India (with historical exceptions for certain territories).
•	Exempts Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, and other groups as notified by the State Government.

2.	Governance and Property Management:- Trustee Appointment: Facilitates the appointment of new trustees by a two-thirds majority in the absence of a provision or feasible existing method.
•	Property Vesting: Automatically vests property in new trustees without requiring a conveyance, subject to the same trusts.
•	Record Keeping: Mandates the recording of new trustee appointments under the Indian Registration Act (referenced as 1877 in the original, but commonly updated to 1908 in practice).

3.	Dissolution: - Permits dissolution by a three-fifths majority of members, with structured provisions for settling the society's affairs.

dc.description.abstract.value:
Summary of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 
Key Provisions
I. Determination of Social Impact & Public Purpose
Social Impact Assessment (SIA) Study:
•	Mandatory before land acquisition (except in specified exemptions).
•	Public hearing for SIA.
•	Publication of SIA report.
Expert Group Appraisal of SIA report.
Exemption from SIA in specified cases (e.g., national security, public health emergencies).
II. Special Provisions
Safeguarding Food Security: Provisions to ensure minimal impact on agricultural land and food security.
III. Notification & Acquisition
Preliminary Notification & Survey:
•	Publication and power of officers to survey.
•	Pre-Acquisition Procedures: Certain actions (e.g., SIA) must be undertaken prior to initiation of acquisition proceedings.
•	Extendable Period for Proceedings Initiation: The appropriate Government can extend the 12-month period for initiating acquisition proceedings if justified, with written record and public notification.
Hearing of Objections within 60 days of notification, covering:
•	Area and suitability of land.
•	Justification for public purpose.
•	SIA report findings.
•	Collector's Role: Receives objections, provides hearing, and submits recommendations to the appropriate Government.
iV. Rehabilitation & Resettlement (R&R)
Preparation of R&R Scheme by the Administrator post preliminary notification:
•	Includes survey, census of affected families, and details on livelihoods, public utilities, and amenities.
•	Draft Scheme Contents:
•	Rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements.
•	List of Government buildings and public amenities in the Resettlement Area.
•	Time-Bound Implementation: Scheme includes a time limit for implementation.
•	Public Participation:
•	Wide publicity and discussion in Gram Sabhas/Municipalities.
•	Mandatory Public Hearing: With adequate publicity, and in every affected Gram Sabha/Municipality if ≥25% of their land is acquired, considering special provisions for Scheduled Areas.
Review of R&R Scheme by the Collector.
V. Compensation
Components of Compensation: - Market value of land.
•	Multiplication factor based on location (rural/urban).
•	Value of assets attached.
•	Solatium (100% of the calculated value).
Determination of Market Value by the Collector.
VI. Judicial & Administrative Provisions
Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority:
•	Establishment.
•	Powers and procedure.
Appeal to High Court from Authority's decisions.
Rules and Regulations: - Power of appropriate Government to make rules.
•	Previous publication of rules.
Power to Remove Difficulties within 2 years of commencement.
Schedules 
•	The First Schedule: Details the minimum compensation package.
•	Provisions for Affected Families: Including those in Scheduled Areas and special considerations for Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
•	Awards and Resettlement Areas: Provisions for infrastructural amenities and corrections to awards.

dc.description.abstract.value:
Summary of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
Objective
The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted to protect wild animals, birds, and plants, conserve their habitats, and maintain ecological and environmental balance. The Act aims to prevent hunting, regulate trade in wildlife and wildlife products, and establish protected areas for the conservation of biodiversity.
Key Provisions
•	Prohibition of Hunting: Prohibits the hunting, capturing, poisoning, or killing of specified wild animals, except in limited circumstances permitted under the Act. 
•	Protected Areas: Provides for the establishment and management of Wildlife Sanctuaries, National Parks, Conservation Reserves, Community Reserves, and Tiger Reserves for wildlife conservation. 
•	Protection of Species: Classifies wild animals and plants into different Schedules, providing varying degrees of protection, with the highest protection for the most endangered species. 
•	Regulation of Trade: Prohibits or regulates the trade, possession, transport, and commerce of wild animals, animal articles, trophies, and specified plants. 
•	Wildlife Authorities: Establishes authorities such as the National Board for Wildlife, State Boards for Wildlife, Chief Wild Life Warden, and other officers for effective implementation of the Act. 
•	Enforcement Powers: Empowers authorized officers to conduct inspections, searches, seizures, arrests, and confiscation of illegally possessed wildlife and wildlife products. 
•	Penalties: Prescribes stringent penalties, including imprisonment and fines, for offences such as illegal hunting, poaching, and unlawful trade in wildlife. 
•	Rule-making Power: Empowers the Central and State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

Discovery by interrogatories. -- (1) In any suit the plaintiff or defendant by leave of the court may deliver interrogatories in writing for the examination of the opposite parties or any one or more of such parties, and such interrogatories when delivered shall have a note at the foot thereof stating which of such interrogatories each of such persons is required to answer:
Provided that no party shall deliver more than one set of interrogatories to the same party without an order for that purpose:
Provided further that interrogatories which do not relate to any matters in question in the suit shall be deemed irrelevant, notwithstanding that they might be admissible on the oral cross-examination of a witness.
(2) On an application for leave to deliver interrogatories, the particular interrogatories proposed to be delivered shall be submitted to the court, and that court shall decide within seven days from the day of filing of the said application, in deciding upon such application, the court shall take into account any offer, which may be made by the party sought to be interrogated to deliver particulars, or to make admissions, or to produce documents relating to the matters in question, or any of them, and leave shall be given as to such only of the interrogatories submitted as the court shall consider necessary either for disposing fairly of the suit or for saving costs.
(3) In adjusting the costs of the suit inquiry shall at the instance of any party be made into the propriety of exhibiting such interrogatories, and if it is the opinion of the taxing officer or of the court, either with or without an application for inquiry, that such interrogatories have been exhibited unreasonably, vexatiously, or at improper length, the costs occasioned by the said interrogatories and the answers thereto shall be paid in any event by the party in fault.
(4) Interrogatories shall be in the form provided in Form No. 2 in Appendix C to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, (5 of 1908) with such variations as circumstances may require.
(5) Where any party to a suit is a corporation or a body of persons, whether incorporated or not, empowered by law to sue or be sued, whether in its own name or in the name of any officer of other person, any opposite party may apply for an order allowing him to deliver interrogatories to any member or officer of such corporation or body, and an order may be made accordingly.
(6) Any objection to answering any interrogatory on the ground that it is scandalous or irrelevant or not exhibited bona fide for the purpose of the suit, or that the matters inquired into are not sufficiently material at that stage, or on the ground of privilege or any other ground may be taken in the affidavit in answer.
(7) Any interrogatories may be set aside on the ground that they have been exhibited unreasonably or vexatiously, or struck out on the ground that they are prolix, oppressive, unnecessary or scandalous and any application for this purpose may be made within seven days after service of the interrogatories.
(8) Interrogatories shall be answered by affidavit to be filed within ten days, or within such other time as the court may allow.
(9) An affidavit in answer to interrogatories shall be in the form provided in Form No. 3 in Appendix C to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, (5 of 1908), with such variations as circumstances may require.

*49. Disputes.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in any law for the time being in force, if any dispute touching the constitution, management or business of a cooperative arises,—
(a) among members, past members and persons claiming through members and deceased members ; or
(b) between a member, past member or a person claiming through a member, past member or deceased member and the cooperative, its board, director, office-bearer, or liquidator, past or present ; or
(c) between the cooperative or its board and any past board, any director, office-bearer, or any past director, past office-bearer, or the nominee, heir, or legal representative of any deceased director or deceased director or deceased office-bearer of the cooperative,
such dispute shall be referred to the arbitral tribunal of the cooperative.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, a dispute shall include :—
(i) a claim by a cooperative for any debt or other amount due to it from a member, past member, the nominee, heir or legal representative of a deceased member, whether such debt or other amount be admitted or not ;
(ii) a claim by surety against the principal debtor where the cooperative has recovered from the surety amount in respect of any debtor or other amount due to it from the principal debtor as a result of the default of the principal debtor whether such debt or amount due be admitted or not ;
(iii) a claim by a cooperative against a member, past member or the nominee, heir or legal representative of a deceased member for the delivery of possession to the cooperative of land or other immovable property resumed by it for breach of the conditions of assignment or allotment of such land or other immovable property.
(2) If any question arises whether a dispute referred to the arbitral tribunal under this section is a dispute touching the constitution, management or business of the cooperative, such question shall be decided by the Arbitral Tribunal.
(3) The Arbitral Tribunal shall decide the dispute in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the articles of association, and such decisions shall be final. Pending final decision on the dispute, the arbitral tribunal may make such interlocutory orders as it may deem necessary in the interest of Justice.
(4) Every order or decision made under this section, shall be executed by the Civil Court having jurisdiction, as if such order is a decree of that Court, on a certificate issued by the Arbitral Tribunal.
(5) Notwithstanding anything in sub-section (4), or in any other law for the time being in force, and without prejudice to any other mode of recovery which is being taken or may be taken, an arbitral tribunal may, on the application made by the cooperative for the recovery of arrears of any sum advanced by the cooperative to any of its members, and on its functioning a statement of accounts in respect of the arrears and after making such inquiry as the tribunal deems fit, issue a certificate for the recovery of the amount stated therein to be due as arrears.
(6) A certificate issued by the arbitral tribunal under sub-section (5) shall be final and conclusive proof of the arrears stated to be due and the certificate shall be executed by the chief executive in the manner specified in the articles of association.
